off.question: A patient on Telma-H develops hyponatremia. Which component is the likely culprit?

must_have: Telma-H is telmisartan + hydrochlorothiazide
Thiazide diuretics (hydrochlorothiazide) are a classic cause of hyponatremia
Management includes stopping/switching the thiazide component and evaluating severity

off.answer:
## Bottom line
In Telma-H (telmisartan + hydrochlorothiazide), the [[F]]hydrochlorothiazide (HCTZ) component is the well-documented culprit for hyponatremia[[/F]], not the telmisartan (ARB) component [1].

## Safety & adverse effects
- Hyponatremia is a recognized, [[F]]dose-related adverse reaction listed in hydrochlorothiazide's own labeling[[/F]] under electrolyte imbalance [2].
- Thiazide diuretics, including HCTZ, are described as a [[F]]"major, common, and potentially life-threatening" cause of drug-induced hyponatremia[[/F]] — "Thiazide-induced hyponatraemia is common and potentially life threatening" [3].
- A retrospective cohort study specifically evaluated hydrochlorothiazide (alongside indapamide and chlorthalidone) in patients admitted with thiazide-associated hyponatremia (TAH), confirming HCTZ as a specific causative agent among thiazides [4].
- Case-level literature reinforces this link, including a case report titled on "hydrochlorothiazide-induced severe hyponatremia" in a habitual beer drinker [5], and older BMJ correspondence on "Hyponatraemia associated with hydrochlorothiazide treatment" [6].
- Combination diuretic labeling (triamterene/HCTZ) similarly lists hyponatremia among electrolyte disturbances associated with the HCTZ component [7].
- [[K]]Elderly patients with low body mass[[/K]] warrant extra caution and close monitoring when prescribed thiazides like HCTZ because of hyponatremia risk [12].
- General clinical guidance states thiazides are a "leading drug cause" of hyponatremia and that management involves stopping the offending diuretic, with SIADH-type hyponatremia treated first with fluid restriction [8][10].
- In contrast, a risk-factor analysis of thiazide-induced hyponatremia found [[R]]no significant association with concomitant ACE inhibitor therapy[[/R]] (a renin-angiotensin-system-acting class related to the ARB telmisartan), indirectly supporting that the RAS-acting component is not the implicated driver [9].

## Population
The evidence pertains to patients receiving thiazide diuretics (hydrochlorothiazide specifically, and related thiazides indapamide/chlorthalidone) [4], with particular caution noted for [[K]]elderly patients with low body mass[[/K]] [12]. No population-specific data are given for the telmisartan component causing hyponatremia.

## Evidence quality
The findings draw on a mix of: drug labeling/prescribing information for hydrochlorothiazide and a triamterene/HCTZ combination (openfda) [2][7]; a retrospective cohort study comparing thiazides in TAH patients [4]; a risk-factor analysis addressing concomitant ACE inhibitor use [9]; case reports/case correspondence [5][6]; and general clinical guidance statements [3][8][10][12]. [[R]]This is predominantly observational/case-level and labeling evidence rather than randomized trial data, but it is highly consistent across sources in implicating the thiazide (HCTZ) component specifically[[/R]], not the ARB.

## Not addressed
The findings do not report a randomized or comparative trial isolating telmisartan's independent effect on serum sodium, nor mechanistic data on why ARBs are not implicated; the conclusion that telmisartan is not the culprit rests on labeling emphasis and an indirect ACE-inhibitor risk-factor analysis rather than direct telmisartan-specific safety data [9].

off.answer:
## Bottom line
The retrieved evidence does not identify what "Redimed-DX" is or contain data on it directly [n/a]; the findings instead cover several unrelated agents (dimenhydrinate, serdexmethylphenidate/dexmethylphenidate, digoxin, dexamethasone, DX-8951f, dexmedetomidine, lisdexamfetamine). Because none of the findings name "Redimed-DX" or establish its interactions with "her current medicines" (which are also not specified in the findings), a safety determination cannot be made from this evidence set [1][2][3][4][5][6][7][8].

## Efficacy
Not addressed — none of the findings report efficacy or outcome data; they cover manufacturing, route of administration, pharmacokinetic/interaction mechanisms, dosing schedule in a trial, and adverse-event reports [1][2][4][5][7][8].

## Safety & adverse effects
- Digoxin has a [[K]]narrow therapeutic index[[/K]] and requires [[F]]increased monitoring of serum digoxin concentrations and for signs/symptoms of clinical toxicity[[/F]] when drugs that interact with it are initiated, adjusted, or discontinued [3].
- Dexamethasone is both a substrate and a [[F]]dose-dependent inducer of CYP3A4[[/F]], a mechanism relevant to drug–drug interactions [4].
- [[F]]Lisdexamfetamine dimesylate (LDX) did not alter CYP1A2, CYP2D6, or CYP3A activity[[/F]] [7], though a small Cmax reduction for omeprazole and its metabolite was observed with LDX co-administration, possibly reflecting an effect on CYP2C19 activity or omeprazole absorption [8].
- FAERS adverse-event reports for PRECEDEX (dexmedetomidine hydrochloride) include [[F]]QT prolongation and T-wave inversion on ECG[[/F]] [6].
- Serdexmethylphenidate and dexmethylphenidate are administered orally [2]; dimenhydrinate is manufactured by Chain Drug Marketing Association, Inc. [1].
- None of these findings mention a product called Redimed-DX, so no adverse-effect or interaction profile for it is established.

## Population
The findings span disparate contexts: an oncology dosing regimen for DX-8951f (IV over 30 minutes daily for 5 days) [5], a FAERS report population for dexmedetomidine [6], and pharmacology studies of lisdexamfetamine's CYP interactions [7][8]. No population is defined for "Redimed-DX" or for the patient's specific current medication regimen.

## Evidence quality
Evidence types are mixed and mostly not comparative: product-label statements (openfda) on digoxin's therapeutic index [3] and dimenhydrinate/serdexmethylphenidate administration [1][2]; a mechanistic pharmacology statement on dexamethasone [4]; a clinical-trial registry entry describing a dosing protocol for DX-8951f, which reflects [[R]]design intent, not efficacy or safety results[[/R]] [5]; a FAERS spontaneous adverse-event report for dexmedetomidine, which is observational/uncontrolled and does not establish causation [6]; and pharmacokinetic interaction studies for lisdexamfetamine [7][8]. None constitutes a systematic review, guideline, or trial result specific to Redimed-DX.

## Not addressed
The findings do not identify "Redimed-DX," its active ingredient(s), or its interaction profile, and do not list the patient's "current medicines." Therefore no direct safety or interaction assessment for the combination asked about can be made from this evidence.

off.question: For a 55-year-old newly diagnosed hypertensive in India, do Indian and international guidelines differ on first-line drug choice?

must_have: Both Indian and international guidance support ACE inhibitors/ARBs, calcium channel blockers, and thiazide-like diuretics as first-line options
Any presentation should state which guidance applies where when recommendations differ (beta-blockers' role, thresholds/targets differ across guidelines)
Amlodipine is commonly favored in Indian practice (heat tolerance, cost, availability considerations)

off.answer:
## Bottom line
Yes — for a 55-year-old newly diagnosed hypertensive, Indian and major international guidelines differ: Indian guidance still frames CCB, ACE inhibitor/ARB, or thiazide as [[F]]first-line drug classes with an emphasis on CCB monotherapy or moderate-dose combinations[[/F]] [2], whereas current international guidance (ISH, ESH 2023, ESC 2024, AHA/ACC 2025) increasingly recommends [[F]]starting most adults directly on a two-drug (ACEi/ARB + CCB) single-pill combination rather than monotherapy[[/F]] [4][5][6][10]. A dedicated comparative review confirms several such deviations exist between Indian and major CPGs [1].

## Efficacy
- **Indian guidance** [2]: first-line classes are CCB (e.g., amlodipine), ACE inhibitor/ARB, or thiazide; CCBs are highlighted as "effective and widely used in Indian practice," with advice to combine drugs at moderate doses rather than maximize a single agent [2]. Diagnostic threshold is ≥140/90 mmHg on repeated measurements, aligned with international thresholds [3].
- **International guidance**:
  - ISH: recommends single-pill ACEi/ARB + CCB combination as first-line for most patients; monotherapy reserved for low-risk grade-1 hypertension or very elderly (≥80)/frail patients [4][10].
  - ESH 2023 / ESC 2024: recommend upfront low-dose combination therapy (preferably single-pill) for most adults with confirmed hypertension, with stepwise escalation from low-dose 2-drug to low-dose 3-drug therapy before maximal triple therapy [5].
  - AHA/ACC 2025: recommends two first-line agents of different classes, preferably fixed-dose combination, for stage 2 hypertension (≥140/90 mmHg) — a threshold [[K]]that would apply to a newly diagnosed 55-year-old at typical presenting BP[[/K]] [6].
  - Broader synthesis: all major guidelines converge on RAS inhibitors (ACEi/ARB), thiazide/thiazide-like diuretics, and CCBs as first-line drug classes, reserving monotherapy for initial/high-normal BP or elderly/frail patients, and favoring low-dose dual combination (ARB/ACEi + CCB or + diuretic) with single-pill/fixed-dose formulations to improve adherence [7]. Combination therapy is also recommended when monotherapy response is inadequate [11].

|---|---|---|

## Safety & adverse effects
The retrieved findings do not report specific adverse-event rates, discontinuation rates, or comparative safety data for CCB/ACEi/ARB/thiazide monotherapy versus combination therapy; no safety figures are available to cite.

## Population
- Findings [2]–[9] concern adults with newly diagnosed/confirmed hypertension, generally consistent with a 55-year-old presenting for initial diagnosis [3][6].
- Indian guidance additionally reflects a **[[K]]primary-care, public-health context[[/K]]** distinct from settings with high baseline hypertension awareness, routine screening, and trained practitioners — i.e., India's Standard Treatment Guidelines (MoHFW, 2016) are explicitly adapted to this different context rather than mirroring international settings [8]. The India Hypertension Control Initiative (IHCI) further emphasizes drug- and dose-specific standardized protocols with task-sharing (nurses, ASHAs) for primary-care follow-up [9][12][13], an implementation layer not centrally featured in the international guideline texts retrieved.
- Exclusions: ISH and Indian guidance both note monotherapy/CCB emphasis differs for very elderly (≥80) or frail patients [4] — not directly the 55-year-old in question, but relevant boundary context.

## Evidence quality
- [[R]]Highest-tier evidence here is guideline-level: ISH, ESH 2023, ESC 2024, AHA/ACC 2025, and Indian CPGs are all consensus clinical practice guidelines, not primary trials, so no individual RCT effect sizes are available in these findings[[/R]] [4][5][6][2].
- A specific comparative review [1] directly assessed concordance between Indian and major international CPGs and reported "several deviations," which is the strongest direct evidence for the question asked.
- India's national Standard Treatment Guidelines were developed following the WHO Handbook for Guideline Development [14], indicating a structured guideline-development process, though the finding does not specify evidence-grading methodology details beyond this.
- No randomized-trial-level efficacy/safety comparisons between Indian-recommended and internationally-recommended first-line strategies are present in these findings; the analysis rests on guideline text comparison rather than outcome trial data.

## Not addressed
The findings do not provide head-to-head trial data comparing CCB/ACEi/ARB/thiazide monotherapy (Indian approach) against upfront ACEi/ARB+CCB combination therapy (international approach) on blood-pressure control or cardiovascular outcomes in Indian patients specifically; nor do they report adverse-event or discontinuation figures for either strategy.

off.question: Suspected diphtheria in a partially vaccinated child in Kerala — immediate management?

must_have: Diphtheria antitoxin should be given on clinical suspicion without waiting for confirmation
Antibiotics (penicillin or erythromycin) plus droplet isolation
Notify public health; give prophylaxis to close contacts and complete vaccination

off.answer:
## Bottom line
Suspected diphtheria — regardless of prior vaccination status — should be treated as a **clinical emergency requiring immediate isolation, empiric diphtheria antitoxin (DAT), and antibiotics before laboratory confirmation** [1][2][3][6]; a partially vaccinated child can still develop clinical disease, so vaccination history should not lower suspicion [19].

## Immediate management (suspicion stage, pre-confirmation)
1. **Isolate immediately**: place in an isolation area with standard, droplet, and contact precautions [[F]]"Place patient immediately in isolation room (or area) and apply standard, droplet and contact precautions"[[/F]] [1].
2. **Give DAT as soon as possible** — do not wait for lab confirmation [2][6]; [[R]]delay matters because diphtheria toxin causes irreversible cellular damage once bound, and antibiotics do not neutralize circulating toxin[[/R]] [11].
3. **Start antibiotics as soon as possible**: penicillin, erythromycin, or azithromycin [3][25]; CDC specifies only erythromycin or penicillin for respiratory/cutaneous disease [7], while WHO's Feb 2024 guideline (2023 West African outbreak context) now recommends macrolides (azithromycin, erythromycin) first-line over penicillin, based on low-certainty evidence [9].
4. **Monitor and support** for airway, cardiac, neurologic, and renal complications [4][26].
5. **Vaccinate** with an age-appropriate diphtheria toxoid-containing vaccine, even though the child is already partially vaccinated, since prior doses do not guarantee full protection [5][19].
6. **Manage close contacts** (household relevance for a child case): quarantine 7–10 days from last exposure, monitor, obtain nasal/throat cultures, give antibiotic prophylaxis (erythromycin or penicillin), and vaccinate anyone not up to date [15]; a partially vaccinated child whose last dose was more than 5 years prior should get an additional dose [15]. If oral compliance is uncertain, use IM benzathine penicillin instead [16].

## Efficacy
- CDC: for **respiratory diphtheria**, DAT "is recommended" [8], alongside antibiotics — "Only erythromycin or penicillin is recommended" [7].
- WHO (Feb 2024 guideline): macrolides preferred first-line over penicillin, "based on low-certainty evidence" [9]; if DAT is unavailable or unlikely accessible quickly, there is a "speculative benefit" to concurrent macrolide + beta-lactam therapy pending susceptibility data [10].
- Standard course: **14 days** of penicillin, erythromycin, or another macrolide plus DAT and hospitalization; timely DAT administration "can prevent potentially irreversible toxin-related damage, reducing mortality rates by up to 76%" [12].
- Illustrative cases: a 10-year-old girl with classic diphtheria, hospitalized 15 days, recovered after antibiotics + DAT [21]; another patient received "one lakh units" of DAT followed by 14 days oral erythromycin, with bulbar symptom improvement (though ptosis persisted) [14][22].
- Outbreak cohort: children received DAT when available, IV benzyl penicillin or erythromycin, corticosteroids for airway edema, and supportive care (oxygen, IV fluids, cardiac monitoring, mechanical ventilation for respiratory failure) [13][23].

## Safety & adverse effects
The findings do not report specific adverse effects of DAT or antibiotics themselves; instead they emphasize disease-related complications requiring monitoring — airway compromise, cardiac, neurologic, and renal failure [4][26] — and a persistent neurologic sequela (ptosis) despite treatment in one case [14]. [[K]]A key real-world safety/logistics issue is drug supply, not drug toxicity[[/K]]: DAT availability is "perilously unreliable" globally, most countries (a category that would include contexts like Kerala) lack stockpiles and rely on donations or UN procurement [18], and in at least one outbreak, confirmed contacts did not receive DAT "due to unavailability" [17].

## Population
Evidence covers **respiratory (and cutaneous) diphtheria** in pediatric and adult patients, including outbreak settings and close contacts of cases [7][13][15][17][20]. It specifically addresses partially/previously vaccinated individuals: [[K]]full vaccination (≥3 doses, DTP series) is reported as 87% effective against symptomatic disease and 81% effective against severe disease, and vaccination reduces transmission by ~60%, but does not eliminate risk of clinical disease or asymptomatic carriage[[/K]] [19]. A single lab-confirmed case is enough to trigger a public health response (contact tracing, active case finding, ring vaccination) [20].

## Evidence quality
- **Guideline-level**: WHO's February 2024 clinical management guideline (developed amid the 2023 West African outbreak) [9][10], and CDC guidance on immediate management, antitoxin/antibiotic choice, and contact management [1][2][3][4][6][7][8][15][16] — these outrank individual case reports.
- [[R]]WHO explicitly labels its macrolide-preference recommendation as based on "low-certainty evidence," so it should be read as a guideline recommendation rather than a high-confidence trial finding[[/R]] [9].
- **Observational/case-level**: an outbreak cohort report [13][17][18][20], and individual case reports [14][21][22] — these are lower-tier evidence illustrating real-world application, not controlled comparisons of regimens.
- No randomized controlled trial data are present among these findings; recommendations rest on guideline consensus and observational/case experience.

## Not addressed
The findings do not include any evidence specific to **Kerala** or the Indian health system's local protocols, drug/antitoxin availability, or reporting requirements — the guidance provided is CDC/WHO-general and outbreak-report-based, not location-specific.

off.question: Which patients qualify for free drugs under the national dialysis / PMNDP-adjacent schemes, and how should I discuss cost of CKD care?

must_have: The Pradhan Mantri National Dialysis Programme provides free/subsidised dialysis in district hospitals
Jan Aushadhi kendras supply low-cost generics
Ayushman Bharat / PM-JAY covers eligible families for hospitalisation including dialysis

off.answer:
## Bottom line
Free/subsidised dialysis in India is targeted mainly at [[K]]BPL (Below Poverty Line) patients[[/K]] through the **Pradhan Mantri National Dialysis Programme (PMNDP)** at district hospitals [1][2][19], with the separate **Ayushman Bharat PM-JAY** scheme extending broader hospitalisation cover (including dialysis) to eligible families [5][12][13]; even with these schemes, out-of-pocket cost for CKD/dialysis care remains substantial and should be discussed explicitly with patients [6][7][8].

## Eligibility / who qualifies
- **PMNDP**: launched to make renal-care services accessible & affordable specifically to **BPL patients** at District Hospitals under NHM [1][19]; covers both **haemodialysis (HD)** and **peritoneal dialysis (PD)** [2][20][11]. Eligibility is not defined by one rigid national criterion beyond BPL status — states are financially supported to extend services "to all the population... including in remote and tribal areas" based on local gap assessments [4].
- **Scale**: as of 30 June 2025, PMNDP operates in **751 districts across all 36 States/UTs**, with **1,704 centres** [3][21].
- **PM-JAY** (Ayushman Bharat, launched 2018): a related but distinct scheme — covers eligible families up to **₹5 lakh/year** for hospitalisation, including dialysis and many surgical/medical packages [5][12][13], and separately pays a **₹1,500 per-session hospital subsidy** for dialysis under health benefit package code **MG072A** [5]. PMJAY has "emerged as one of the most important methods of subsidizing dialysis" [14], with enrollment among hemodialysis patients rising from **25.3% at initiation to 78.7%** later in the course of treatment [6][17].
- **Jan Aushadhi**: a separate scheme providing low-cost generic medicines that can be combined with dialysis/insurance coverage to improve affordability of chronic CKD drug therapy [9].

## Cost burden — what to discuss with patients
- [[F]]Scheme coverage does not eliminate out-of-pocket burden[[/F]]: despite PM-JAY uptake rising to 78.7%, patients on maintenance hemodialysis still incur substantial costs [6].
- A Central India study of stable hemodialysis patients found **median monthly out-of-pocket expenditure of INR 17,058.3 (IQR: 11,922.9–26,672.9)**, and **three-fourths of patients had to borrow money** to cover healthcare costs [7].
- Roughly three-fourths of this out-of-pocket spend is **direct medical cost** (medication, private dialysis sessions, erythropoietin injections, blood transfusion), with about one-fourth indirect (transport, food) [8] — worth flagging that drug/medication costs are a major, persistent component even under subsidy.
- **Distance/access** compounds cost burden: median travel distance to dialysis was **30 km (IQR: 7–85 km)** [10][15], and rising demand is not fully met by existing public infrastructure, prompting calls to expand dialysis centers into PHCs and district hospitals [18]. Some patients (33 in one cohort) started at private facilities and transitioned to public ones after a mean of 19 months [16], illustrating a pathway toward lower-cost care over time.

## Evidence quality
The PMNDP scale/eligibility figures come from web-sourced government program descriptions [1][2][3][4][19][20][21] and a guideline-style summary [11] — programmatic/administrative reporting, not clinical trial evidence. The PM-JAY cost-burden and enrollment data [6][7][8][10][15][16][17] derive from a single observational study (n=99 hemodialysis patients [15]) — [[R]]cross-sectional/observational data describing real-world expenditure and scheme uptake, not a controlled comparison of cost outcomes with vs without scheme enrollment[[/R]]. No systematic review or RCT evidence on scheme eligibility or cost-effectiveness is present in these findings.

## Not addressed
The findings do not specify exact income thresholds, documentation, or a step-by-step enrollment process defining "BPL" or PM-JAY eligibility; nor do they provide a controlled comparison of out-of-pocket cost with versus without scheme coverage, or national-level (vs single-region) cost data.

on.question: 45-year-old in Delhi with fever for 4 days, platelet count 90,000, and severe abdominal pain with persistent vomiting. Dengue NS1 positive. Can I send him home with paracetamol?

must_have: Abdominal pain and persistent vomiting are WARNING SIGNS in dengue requiring admission/close observation, not home management
NSAIDs and aspirin must be avoided in dengue
Monitoring (serial hematocrit/platelets, watch for plasma leakage as defervescence approaches) is required

on.answer:
## Bottom line
No — this patient should **not** be sent home. He has dengue fever with [[K]]warning signs[[/K]] (severe abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, platelet count 90,000) [1][2], and both WHO-2009-based and CDC guidance state that dengue patients with warning signs require **inpatient management**, not outpatient paracetamol [3][4].

## Efficacy / Applicable guidance
This is a triage/management question rather than a drug-efficacy question, so the relevant "evidence" is classification and disposition criteria:

- **Warning-sign criteria (WHO 2009, reflected in CDC guidance):** severe/persistent abdominal pain and persistent vomiting are explicitly listed warning signs of dengue at risk of progressing to severe disease [1]; CDC operationalizes persistent vomiting as **≥3 episodes/hr or ≥4 episodes in 6 hrs** [2]. This patient has both severe abdominal pain and persistent vomiting [1][2].
- **Platelet count:** his count of 90,000 falls within the thrombocytopenia associated with the warning-signs category [1], and a comparable South Asian (Bangladesh) national protocol treats platelet count **≤100,000/mm³** (with rising hematocrit) as a warning sign requiring closer attention [8] — consistent with, though not identical to, this patient's 90,000 count.
- **Disposition rule:** [[F]]"Dengue patients with warning signs should be managed as inpatients"[[/F]] [3][4]. Outpatient management with acetaminophen is reserved only for dengue **without** warning signs in hemodynamically stable patients tolerating oral fluids [5][6] — a category this patient does not meet [1][2].
- Paracetamol (acetaminophen) is confirmed as the antipyretic/analgesic of choice for dengue pain generally, but the same source states severe cases require hospitalization and there is no specific antiviral treatment [7].

## Safety & adverse effects
- Aspirin and NSAIDs (e.g., ibuprofen) should be avoided in dengue because they can increase bleeding risk [6][7] — this applies regardless of inpatient/outpatient status.
- No adverse effects of paracetamol itself are reported in these findings; the safety concern here is disease trajectory, not drug toxicity: warning-sign patients are "at increased risk of progressing to severe dengue" [1].

## Population
- Findings apply to dengue patients classified per **WHO 2009 criteria** as having warning signs (abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, fluid accumulation, mucosal bleeding, lethargy, hepatomegaly, rising hematocrit, thrombocytopenia) [1][2] — this patient's presentation matches this category [1][2].
- The outpatient/home-management pathway with paracetamol applies to a **different population**: hemodynamically stable dengue patients without warning signs, tolerating oral fluids, without significant comorbidities [5][6] — not applicable here.
- A comparable warning-sign threshold (platelet ≤100,000/mm³ with rising hematocrit) comes from a Bangladesh national protocol [8], useful as a regional parallel but not an India-specific guideline in these findings.

## Evidence quality
- The core disposition rule ("manage as inpatient") is stated identically by two CDC-guideline-based sources, both grounded in the **WHO 2009 classification** — a guideline-tier source, the highest tier in the hierarchy for this question [3][4][1][2].
- WHO global guidance corroborates paracetamol as standard symptomatic care but affirms hospitalization for severe cases [7].
- The platelet-threshold cross-reference comes from a national pocket-guideline/observational description (Bangladesh) rather than a systematic review or RCT [8], so it is supportive/parallel evidence rather than the primary basis for the decision.
- No findings here are India-specific (ICMR/NVBDCP) guidance; the applicable guidance identified is CDC/WHO-based [1][2][3][4][7].

## Not addressed
The findings do not include India-specific (ICMR/NVBDCP) dengue treatment guidelines, do not report outcomes data for patients discharged despite warning signs, and do not address alternative diagnoses (e.g., typhoid/enteric fever findings [9][10][11][12] are not tied to this patient's NS1-positive dengue diagnosis and are not applicable here).

on.question: Farmer bitten by a snake an hour ago, brought with progressive ptosis and difficulty breathing. What do I give?

must_have: Anti-snake venom (polyvalent ASV) is indicated for signs of systemic envenomation such as neurotoxicity
Neostigmine (with atropine) may be used for neurotoxic envenomation
Airway/ventilatory support readiness is essential
Do NOT apply tourniquets or incise/suck the wound

on.answer:
## Bottom line
This is [[K]]clinical neurotoxic snake envenoming[[/K]] (progressive ptosis, respiratory difficulty) [1] — treat as a medical emergency: give [[F]]polyvalent anti-snake venom (ASV) early[[/F]], alongside neostigmine and atropine, and prepare for airway/ventilatory support, per Indian national guidance [2][4]. Do not waste time on tourniquets, incision, or suction — reassure, immobilize, and transfer/treat rapidly [3].

## Efficacy / Management (India-applicable guidance)
- **Antivenom (ASV):** Definitive treatment for systemic envenomation is polyvalent ASV [2][20]. Antivenom should be given early on clinical judgment, without waiting for confirmation [14]; [[R]]delay worsens outcomes[[/R]] [15], and antivenom is most effective before full-blown paralysis develops [16] — relevant since ptosis is already progressing in this patient.
- **Neostigmine + Atropine:** Used per National Health Mission-referenced practice to reverse neuromuscular blockade and manage ptosis, diplopia, dysphagia, and respiratory distress: neostigmine 0.5–1 mg IV (reverses neuromuscular blockade, dose adjusted to paralysis severity) and atropine 0.5–1 mg IV (for bradycardia/secretions) [4][19][2]. In one case, a second ASV dose (10 vials) was given together with atropine and neostigmine [17].
- **Calcium gluconate:** In suspected krait bites specifically, calcium gluconate 10–20 mL of 10% solution IV was given adjunctively to stabilize the neuromuscular junction [5]. Urgent ASV is recommended for proven krait bites regardless of neurotoxic symptoms [24].
- **Dosing intensity:** Evidence on high- vs low-dose ASV is mixed and not from India:
  - A Nepal RCT comparing low (2 vials) vs high (10 vials) initial ASV dose found the high dose was **not more effective** than low dose, and the antivenom used performed poorly overall [9][10].
  - A separate retrospective study of 55 ventilated patients found low-dose (150 mL) and high-dose (100 mL then 100 mL q6h, median total 600 mL) regimens had similar outcomes — 3 deaths in the high-dose group, 2 with neurological sequelae in the low-dose group, others recovered without deficit [11][21].
- **WHO position:** Early administration of an adequate antivenom dose in a patient with signs of envenoming is crucial; if antivenom is unavailable, rapid referral or ABC-focused symptomatic care should be prioritized [7]. Early antivenom use is associated with faster recovery and shorter hospital stay [23].
- **If paralysis is advanced:** Once neurotoxic signs/nerve terminal damage are established, antivenom becomes less effective, and respiratory muscle involvement requires immediate intubation and mechanical ventilation [8].

## Safety & adverse effects
| Agent | Reported issue | Management |
|---|---|---|
| ASV | Anaphylaxis (monitor during infusion) [2]; pulmonary edema (toxin-mediated capillary leak or anaphylactic) [12] | Hydrocortisone + chlorpheniramine for suspected anaphylaxis; IV furosemide for pulmonary edema, with improved oxygenation reported in one case [13][18] |
| High- vs low-dose ASV | No difference in treatment-related adverse events between high- and low-dose groups in the Nepal RCT [25] | High initial dose offers single-dosing convenience without added risk [10] |

[[F]]Anaphylaxis and pulmonary edema are recognized ASV complications[[/F]] requiring active monitoring and prompt treatment [12][13].

## Population
Findings apply to patients with **clinical neurotoxic envenoming** (ptosis, diplopia, dysphagia, respiratory distress), including suspected krait bites [1][4][5][24], and to severe cases requiring ventilation [6][11]. Dosing-comparison evidence comes from Nepal (Indian polyvalent antivenom) [9][10] and an unspecified cohort of 55 ventilated patients [11] — not specifically Indian farmers or a defined time-since-bite population; this patient is 1 hour post-bite, which the findings do not separately analyze.

## Evidence quality
- [[R]]Indian national guidance (india_guidelines) on ASV + neostigmine/atropine [2][20] and WHO guidance [7] sit at the top of the hierarchy and should govern practice in India.[[/R]]
- The Nepal antivenom-dosing comparison is a randomized controlled trial [9][10], outranking the retrospective 55-patient dosing study [11] and the case-report/case-series level evidence on ASV complications and specific drug management [4][5][12][13][17][18] (europepmc).
- Findings [14]–[16] and [22]–[23] are stated as general clinical principles/reviews without further named study detail.

## Not addressed
The findings do not give a time-since-bite-specific protocol (e.g., whether management differs at 1 hour vs later) [1]; they do not name the snake species for this case; and there is no Indian-specific RCT dosing comparison for ASV (dosing RCTs cited are from Nepal) [9][10][11].

on.question: Stray dog bite with bleeding wound on the hand in an unvaccinated adult. Post-exposure steps?

must_have: Category III exposure: immediate thorough wound washing with soap and water
Rabies immunoglobulin infiltrated into and around the wound
Full course of anti-rabies vaccine (intradermal or intramuscular per national schedule)

on.answer:
## Bottom line
A stray dog bite with a bleeding wound on the hand in an unvaccinated adult is a **Category III exposure** [1], which per India-applicable guidance requires **immediate wound washing, a full rabies vaccine course, AND rabies immunoglobulin (RIG) infiltrated into the wound** — vaccine alone is not sufficient [13][19]. Bleeding at the wound site specifically flags a potentially severe exposure that must receive immunoglobulin infiltration [2].

## Efficacy / recommended steps
1. **Immediate wound care**: Wash and flush the wound thoroughly with soap/detergent and copious water for about [[F]]15 minutes[[/F]], then apply an iodine-containing (or similarly viricidal) topical preparation if available [3]. This should be done immediately in all category III exposures [19].
2. **Rabies immunoglobulin (RIG)**: Because bleeding indicates potentially severe exposure, RIG (human or equine) must be infiltrated into the wound [2][17]. RIG is infiltrated **into the depth and around the wound** as much as anatomically feasible, with any remainder given intramuscularly at a site distant from the vaccine (e.g., anterior thigh) [4]. Dosing: [[F]]20 IU/kg for human RIG or 40 IU/kg for equine RIG[[/F]], and the total recommended dose should not be exceeded [5]. If RIG is unavailable at the first visit, it can be given up to **7 days** after the first vaccine dose [6].
3. **Rabies vaccine**: A full course of rabies vaccine injections should be started promptly [7][18], and PEP should not be delayed pending laboratory diagnosis or animal observation [7].
4. **Wound suturing**: If suturing is required, it should be done loosely and only *after* RIG has been infiltrated into the wound [8].
5. **Adjunct care**: Antibiotics and tetanus prophylaxis are also part of supportive management [10].
6. **Animal-dependent discontinuation**: PEP should proceed even if the stray dog is unavailable for testing/observation [9]. It may only be discontinued later if the dog is confirmed vaccinated and remains healthy after **10 days of observation**, or tests negative by a WHO-prescribed laboratory test [9] — a scenario that does not directly apply to an unowned stray unless it can be captured and observed.

## Safety & adverse effects
- The findings note that patients receiving rabies monoclonal antibodies (an alternative to RIG) experienced only **mild adverse events** that resolved spontaneously or with symptomatic treatment, without complications [16]; this pertains to monoclonal antibody products rather than conventional human/equine RIG specifically.
- No adverse-effect data for standard human/equine RIG or the vaccine itself are given in these findings.

## Population
These recommendations apply specifically to **Category III exposure** — transdermal bites/scratches or mucous-membrane/broken-skin contamination with saliva from a suspected rabid animal [1] — in an **unvaccinated adult** [13]. The stray, unobserved status of the dog means PEP should not be withheld or delayed pending the animal's availability [9].

## Evidence quality
[[K]]India-applicable guidance[[/K]] (labeled "india_guidelines") directly states the Category III unvaccinated-person requirement for combined vaccine + RIG + washing [13], concordant with WHO-referenced web guidance on category III management, RIG dosing/technique, timing, and suturing [1]–[9][17][19]. [[R]]This is guideline-level/protocol-directed care rather than a single trial's efficacy result — it does not report outcome rates (e.g., survival, seroconversion) for a specific completed trial, so it should be read as recommended practice, not as an effect-size finding[[/R]]. Supporting observational/case-report evidence highlights real-world adherence gaps: fewer than [[F]]2% of Category III bite victims in low- and middle-income countries receive immunoglobulin[[/F]] [11][15], and case series (case-report level) document rabies deaths from improper suturing and omitted RIG despite vaccination [12][14].

## Not addressed
The findings do not report clinical outcome data (e.g., rabies incidence, survival rates) specifically for a hand-bite Category III exposure cohort, nor any comparative efficacy data for human vs equine RIG or for monoclonal antibody products against conventional RIG in this population.

on.question: Pregnant woman at 20 weeks with hemoglobin 9.5 g/dL. How should I manage her anemia per the national programme?

must_have: Moderate/mild anemia in pregnancy is treated with therapeutic oral iron-folic acid (e.g. 2 IFA tablets daily under Anemia Mukt Bharat)
Reassess hemoglobin after 4 weeks(ish) of therapy
Injectable iron (iron sucrose/FCM) or referral applies for non-response or severe anemia; deworming (albendazole) is part of the programme

on.answer:
## Bottom line
At Hb 9.5 g/dL and 20 weeks, this patient has **moderate anemia** by both trimester-specific and universal cutoffs [1][2]. Under India's Anemia Mukt Bharat (AMB)/NHM programme, moderate anemia in pregnancy is managed with **therapeutic oral iron and follow-up**, reserving parenteral iron or transfusion for severe anemia or oral-iron non-response/intolerance [3].

## Efficacy
- **Classification confirms moderate anemia**: second-trimester moderate anemia is defined as 7.0–9.4 g/dL [1] (note: 9.5 g/dL falls just above this band and within the "mild" 9.5–10.4 g/dL range by the trimester-specific scheme [1], but is within the "moderate" band 7.0–9.9 g/dL under the older/universal classification also cited in national guidance [2]).
- **First-line therapy — oral iron**: [[F]]National programme guidance directs therapeutic oral iron with follow-up for moderate anemia[[/F]] [3], consistent with FIGO's evidence-based recommendation of **60–120 mg elemental iron daily** as first-line treatment for iron deficiency anemia in pregnancy, continued until Hb normalizes to ≥11.0 g/dL, then reduced to a prophylactic dose (30–60 mg) for 3 months or 6 weeks postpartum, whichever is longer [7].
- **India-specific dosing note**: a landmark Indian RCT (Reddaiah et al., 1989) supported 120 mg elemental iron over the WHO-recommended 60 mg, and this higher dose was adopted in the National Nutritional Anemia Prophylaxis Programme [9]. A systematic review, however, found ambiguity/lack of consensus on the ideal prophylactic iron dose [12].
- **Alternative dosing threshold**: separate guidance recommends 60–120 mg supplemental iron when Hb is 9.0–10.9 g/dL and ferritin <12 µg/L [18], which is consistent with this patient's Hb range.
- **Universal prophylaxis backbone**: regardless of anemia grade, daily iron-folic acid (IFA) supplementation is mandated through pregnancy and lactation, with Hb screened at ANC visits [4], and is recommended globally as a public-health intervention to reduce maternal anemia [11][19].
- **Escalation pathway**: if oral iron is poorly tolerated or ineffective, MoHFW's Operational Guidelines on IV Iron (under AMB) permit IV iron (e.g., Ferric Carboxymaltose [FCM] or Iron Sucrose [IS]) for **moderate to severe** anemia [5][17]. FCM is noted to give a faster Hb rise, shorter infusion time, and fewer side effects, making it "especially beneficial in the second and third trimesters" [6] — [[K]]directly relevant since this patient is at 20 weeks[[/K]], should oral therapy fail.

## Safety & adverse effects
- Parenteral iron per FIGO guidance is indicated only for non-response, non-compliance, or intolerance to oral iron, or for moderate-to-severe iron deficiency anemia; it is **not recommended in the first trimester** owing to limited safety data — not a concern here at 20 weeks [8].
- **Blood transfusion** is reserved for severe anemia (especially near term), acute severe bleeding, or hemodynamic/cardiac compromise [10] — [[F]]not indicated at Hb 9.5 g/dL at 20 weeks[[/F]].
- No adverse-effect data for oral iron dosing itself are reported in these findings beyond the comparative note that FCM has "fewer side effects" than implied alternatives in second/third trimester use [6].

## Population
- Findings apply specifically to **pregnant women** classified with anemia by trimester-specific or universal Hb cutoffs [1][2], within the **Indian national programme context** (Anemia Mukt Bharat/NHM) [3][4][5][16].
- The IV iron escalation and FCM benefit apply to **moderate to severe** anemia and are specifically flagged as beneficial in **second and third trimester** [5][6] — matching this patient's 20-week gestation.
- Parenteral iron is explicitly **not** indicated in the first trimester [8], a caveat not relevant here but defining the boundary of applicability.

## Evidence quality
[[R]]The Indian national programme guidance [3][4][5] is a **programmatic/policy-level guideline** (MoHFW Operational Guidelines under AMB/NHM) and is the directly governing standard for practice in India, taking precedence for this question.[[/R]] It is supported by FIGO evidence-based recommendations [7][8][10], which are graded (e.g., "strong, low"; "strong, high"), indicating variable underlying evidence certainty despite strong recommendation strength. The 120 mg dosing precedent [9] derives from a single named RCT (Reddaiah et al., 1989) later adopted into the national programme — [[R]]a historical trial-derived policy choice, not a recent head-to-head efficacy comparison[[/R]]. A systematic review [12] highlights unresolved uncertainty on optimal prophylactic dosing, tempering confidence in exact dose figures. No completed-trial efficacy results for IV iron vs oral iron in this exact scenario are provided in these findings; the IV iron guidance [5][6][17] is programmatic/operational rather than trial-outcome evidence.

## Not addressed
The findings do not report actual Hb-response outcomes, timelines, or adverse-event rates for oral iron treatment specifically in a 20-week, Hb 9.5 g/dL patient, nor a head-to-head trial comparing oral vs IV iron in this exact population.

on.question: 6-month-old with acute watery diarrhoea, some dehydration. What does the national programme recommend?

must_have: ORS (low-osmolarity) is the mainstay of rehydration
Zinc supplementation for 14 days (10 mg <6 months, 20 mg >=6 months)
Continue feeding/breastfeeding; antibiotics only for dysentery/cholera-type indications

on.answer:
## Bottom line
For a 6-month-old with acute watery diarrhoea and **some dehydration (Plan B)**, the applicable national/programme guidance (India's ICMR Standard Treatment Workflow, consistent with WHO's Pocket Book) recommends [[F]]oral rehydration with ORS at 75 ml/kg over 4 hours in a clinic/day-care setting[[/F]] [1][12], plus **zinc supplementation for 14 days** [[F]]at 20 mg/day (since the child is ≥6 months)[[/F]] [9], and continued feeding/breastfeeding [9][4], with **no routine antibiotics** [10][7].

## Efficacy / Recommended management
- **Fluid management (Plan B):** "Manage in clinic/daycare facility with recommended amount of ORS (75ml/kg) over 4hour period" [1]. Age/weight-banded ORS tables are used to determine volumes for the first 4 hours [2][13]; for the 4-to-≤12-month band (which covers a 6-month-old), the amount is [[F]]400–700 ml over 4 hours[[/F]] [13]. If the child wants more than this amount, more should be given [14].
- **Reassessment:** After 4 hours, the child must be reassessed and reclassified for dehydration to select the next plan (A/B/C) [2][15][3].
- **Zinc:** All children with diarrhoea should receive zinc [6]; the Indian programme specifies [[F]]10 mg/day for <6 months and 20 mg/day for ≥6 months, for 14 days[[/F]] [9] — for this 6-month-old, the 20 mg/day dose applies [9].
- **Feeding:** Continued feeding/breastfeeding is part of the core regimen, alongside ORS and zinc [9], and breastfeeding should continue during ORS administration [5].
- **Home-care counselling:** The "four rules of home treatment" — extra fluid, zinc, continued feeding, and knowing when to return — should be explained to caregivers [5].
- **Broader programme context:** India's 2024 STOP Diarrhoea Campaign provides co-packaged ORS (two packets) and zinc to all under-five children as part of a two-month strategy [8], reflecting programmatic delivery of the same ORS+zinc regimen described above [8][9].

## Safety & adverse effects
- **Antibiotics:** [[F]]Not recommended routinely[[/F]] for acute watery diarrhoea; reserved for dysentery (blood in stool) or suspected cholera with severe dehydration, or serious non-intestinal infections such as pneumonia/UTI [10][7].
- **Antidiarrhoeal/anti-emetic drugs:** Should **not** be given to young children with acute or persistent diarrhoea — "they do not prevent dehydration or improve nutritional status, and some have dangerous, sometimes fatal, side-effects" [7].
- **Referral triggers if condition worsens:** [[K]]Severe dehydration, hypernatremic (Na >145 mmol/L)/hyponatremic (Na <135 mmol/L) dehydration, dysentery with age <1 year or with dehydration, or persistent diarrhoea with dehydration warrant hospital referral[[/K]] [3]. Danger signs — unable to drink, lethargy, persistent vomiting, sunken eyes with poor skin pinch — indicate severe dehydration and referral for IV fluids [11].

## Population
This guidance applies to **infants and young children with acute watery diarrhoea classified as having "some dehydration" (Plan B)** [1][12], with the ORS-volume table specifically covering the 4-to-≤12-month/6–<10 kg band relevant to a 6-month-old [13]. It does **not** apply as-is to severe dehydration (Plan C) or no dehydration (Plan A), nor to dysentery, cholera, or severely malnourished/HIV-positive children, who fall under separate referral criteria [3][11].

## Evidence quality
[[R]]The recommendations rest on national programme/standard treatment guidance (ICMR Standard Treatment Workflow, India-specific dosing table) and align with WHO's Pocket Book of Hospital Care for Children, which underpins IMNCI — i.e., guideline-level evidence rather than individual trial data[[/R]] [1][4][9]. The India-specific zinc dosing (10 mg vs 20 mg by age) is drawn from national guidelines [9], and programmatic scale-up (STOP Diarrhoea Campaign) is described in a peer-reviewed/indexed source (Europe PMC) [8]. No individual randomized trial results are cited in these findings; the evidence is guideline/programme-derived rather than primary trial data.

## Not addressed
The findings do not report trial-level efficacy data (e.g., reduction in stool output, diarrhoea duration, or mortality) for ORS/zinc in this age group, nor any adverse-event rates from the national programme itself.

on.question: 14-year-old with confirmed rheumatic fever with carditis. What secondary prophylaxis and for how long?

must_have: Benzathine penicillin G intramuscularly every 3-4 weeks (commonly every 21 days in India)
With carditis, prophylaxis continues at least 10 years or until age 25 (whichever is longer); lifelong with residual valve disease per severity
Penicillin allergy alternative: oral erythromycin/macrolide

on.answer:
## Bottom line
For a 14-year-old with confirmed acute rheumatic fever (ARF) and carditis, secondary prophylaxis is [[F]]regular benzathine penicillin G (BPG) injections every 3–4 weeks[[/F]] [1], continued for [[F]]10 years from the last ARF episode or until age 21, whichever is longer[[/F]] if there is no detectable persistent heart disease [2][15], or [[F]]10 years from the last episode or until age 40, whichever is longer[[/F]] if there is detectable persistent rheumatic heart disease (RHD) [3][14]. For a 14-year-old, both thresholds extend well past age 21/40 respectively given the "whichever is longer" rule [2].

## Efficacy / Regimen
- **Agent and interval:** Benzathine penicillin G, given intramuscularly every 3–4 weeks, is the WHO-recommended and AHA-endorsed regimen for secondary prophylaxis [1][12].
- **Duration depends on carditis status:**

| Clinical status | Recommended duration |
|---|---|
| No evidence of carditis | 5 y from last ARF episode or until age 21, whichever is longer [16] |
| Carditis, no detectable persistent heart disease | 10 y from last ARF episode or until age 21, whichever is longer [2][15] |
| Carditis with detectable persistent heart disease (RHD) | 10 y from last ARF episode or until age 40, whichever is longer [3][14] |

- This patient (confirmed carditis) falls into one of the latter two rows depending on whether persistent (echocardiographic/clinical) heart disease is documented [2][3][14][15].
- A concordant source states that "for patients with carditis, even when subclinical, current guidelines recommend benzathine penicillin every three to four weeks for at least 10 years or until 21 years of age, whichever is longer" [5][9], reinforcing the 10-year/age-21 floor regardless of whether disease is overt.
- **Alternative WHO framing:** WHO's general guidance states prophylaxis should continue "for at least five years after the last episode of ARF or until the age of 18 years (whichever is longer) and for a greater length of time in case of carditis or RHD" [4][10] — i.e., the 5-year/age-18 rule is the floor for ARF without carditis, with carditis specifically requiring longer duration, consistent with the 10-year rules above.
- **National variation:** Australian guidelines specify prophylaxis to age 18 or 5 years post-episode (whichever longer) for those without carditis, but "up to the age of 40" for those with severe RHD [7], illustrating that duration escalates with carditis/RHD severity across guideline bodies.
- Separately, the *duration of anti-inflammatory treatment* (not antibiotic prophylaxis) for children with severe carditis was reported as 12 weeks [13] — this is a distinct treatment from secondary antibiotic prophylaxis and should not be conflated with it.

## Safety & adverse effects
- No specific adverse-effect data for BPG itself are reported in these findings.
- [[K]]Adherence, not drug toxicity, is flagged as the principal safety/effectiveness challenge[[/K]]: "BPG is only effective with high adherence, which remains a major challenge due to poor compliance in many settings," and poor adherence is a significant risk factor for ARF recurrence [8].
- **Penicillin-allergic patients:** sulfadiazine or a macrolide/azalide are acceptable alternatives to penicillin for secondary prophylaxis [6][17].

## Population
- Findings apply to patients diagnosed with ARF per Jones criteria (major/minor clinical criteria ± evidence of prior GAS infection) [18], across the spectrum from no carditis to carditis with or without persistent (RHD) findings [2][3][15][16].
- [[K]]Carditis may be subclinical, detectable only by echocardiography, and if missed can progress to chronic RHD[[/K]] — relevant to correctly classifying a patient's duration tier [19].
- The 14-year-old in question falls under the "carditis" categories [2][3][14][15]; the specific duration (age-21 vs age-40 threshold) depends on whether persistent heart disease is detectable, which these findings do not resolve for this specific patient.

## Evidence quality
- [[R]]The core recommendations derive from WHO guidance and AHA scientific statement–level sources, which sit at the guideline tier of the evidence hierarchy and are the appropriate authority for duration/agent recommendations[[/R]] [1][4][6][10][17].
- A named guideline-derived duration table (carditis with/without persistent heart disease; no carditis) is used consistently across multiple citations [2][3][14][15][16], increasing confidence that this reflects an authoritative, reproduced guideline table rather than a single study's finding.
- Australian national guidance is cited as an example of country-level variation, not as evidence overriding WHO/AHA recommendations [7].
- Adherence and cost-effectiveness statements come from a review-type synthesis in europepmc, characterizing programmatic challenges rather than reporting a specific trial [8][11].
- No individual RCT of prophylaxis duration or regimen is cited; the findings reflect guideline synthesis, which outranks single-trial evidence for a "what should be given" question.

## Not addressed
The findings do not specify how to determine, in this specific 14-year-old, whether "detectable persistent heart disease" is present (e.g., echocardiographic criteria) — which determines whether the age-21 or age-40 duration threshold applies [2][3][14][15][19].

on.question: Adult from Bihar with 3 weeks of fever, splenomegaly and pancytopenia; rK39 positive. First-line treatment under the kala-azar programme?

must_have: Single-dose liposomal amphotericin B (10 mg/kg IV) is the programme first-line for visceral leishmaniasis in India
Miltefosine or amphotericin deoxycholate are alternatives
Post-treatment follow-up for relapse and PKDL is required

on.answer:
## Bottom line
For an adult from **Bihar** with fever >3 weeks, splenomegaly, pancytopenia and a positive rK39 test — meeting the case definition for visceral leishmaniasis (VL/kala-azar) under India's elimination programme — the first-line treatment is [[F]]a single intravenous infusion of liposomal amphotericin B at 10 mg/kg body weight[[/F]] [1][2][5], with combination paromomycin-miltefosine for 10 days as an alternative regimen under the programme [1].

## Efficacy
- **India national guidance (applies here):** In the Indian focus, [[F]]single-dose liposomal amphotericin B is the preferred first-line treatment; antimonials are not recommended owing to high resistance[[/F]] [5]. National guidelines specify a single IV infusion at 10 mg/kg after excluding HIV co-infection [2][8].
- **Program-level case definition and options:** Anyone with fever >2 weeks plus spleno/hepatomegaly in an endemic area with lab confirmation is treated with single-dose liposomal amphotericin B (10 mg/kg) or a 10-day paromomycin-miltefosine combination [1].
- **Bihar-specific trial evidence:** A large randomized trial conducted in [[K]]Bihar, where a majority of India's VL cases occur[[/K]], found single-infusion liposomal amphotericin B (10 mg/kg) [[F]]not inferior to, and less expensive than, conventional 15-dose amphotericin B deoxycholate[[/F]], with cure rates at 6 months of 95.7% (95% CI 93.4–97.9) vs 96.3% (95% CI 92.6–99.9); apparent cure at day 30 was 100% (304/304) with liposomal therapy vs 98% (106/108) with conventional therapy [6].
- Consistent with this, liposomal amphotericin B given as a single dose is reported to have an efficacy of more than 95% for kala-azar [7][9].
- **Regional adoption:** Bangladesh adopted single-dose liposomal amphotericin B as first-line VL treatment in 2012, followed by India and Nepal [3]; two decades into the elimination initiative, it remains the drug of choice, with rK39 as the key diagnostic [4].

## Safety & adverse effects
- The Indian guidelines note antimonials are **not recommended** owing to high resistance [5] — implying liposomal amphotericin B is favored partly on this safety/efficacy trade-off, though no specific antimonial adverse-effect figures are given in these findings.
- HIV co-infection is excluded before treatment per national guidelines, indicating this is a relevant screening step before administering liposomal amphotericin B [2][8].
- In a special population — VL-associated hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH) — intravenous dexamethasone has been used alongside a six-day course of liposomal amphotericin B [10]; this is not the standard uncomplicated-VL regimen and is not described as programme-standard.
- No adverse-event rates for liposomal amphotericin B itself (e.g., infusion reactions, nephrotoxicity) are reported in these findings.

## Population
These findings apply to **adults/patients in VL-endemic areas of India** (notably Bihar, where most of India's VL burden occurs) [6], diagnosed via the programme's clinical case definition (fever >2 weeks, splenomegaly/hepatomegaly) plus laboratory confirmation (rK39) [1][4][7]. HIV co-infection is explicitly excluded before this standard regimen is given [2][8]. The HLH-related dexamethasone regimen applies only to a distinct complicated subgroup [10], not the general kala-azar case as described in the question.

## Evidence quality
- [[R]]Indian national/programme guidance (findings [1], [2], [5], [8]) represents the applicable practice standard for India and should be followed directly for this case[[/R]].
- The Bihar trial [6] is a completed randomized trial with reported outcome data (cure rates, CIs) — the strongest individual-study evidence here, and it directly supports the guideline recommendation.
- Findings [3], [4], [7], [9] are narrative/summary statements (e.g., regional adoption history, general efficacy statements) that corroborate but do not independently establish new efficacy data beyond the trial in [6].
- Finding [10] is a single case-level description (HLH complication) and does not generalize to standard first-line dosing.

## Not addressed
The findings do not report adverse-event rates or safety profile specifics for liposomal amphotericin B (e.g., infusion reactions, nephrotoxicity, relapse rates) in the general Bihar/Indian VL population, nor do they address treatment outcomes specifically in patients presenting with pancytopenia as a described feature.

on.question: Fever with eschar on the groin in a farm worker from the Northeast during monsoon; suspicion of scrub typhus. Empiric therapy?

must_have: Doxycycline 100 mg twice daily is first-line empiric therapy
Azithromycin is the alternative (pregnancy, children where preferred)
Defervescence within 48 hours supports the diagnosis; complications (ARDS, AKI, meningoencephalitis) need escalation

on.answer:
## Bottom line
For a patient in whom scrub typhus is clinically suspected (fever plus an eschar, in an epidemiologically consistent setting such as a farm worker in the Northeast during monsoon), [[F]]empiric doxycycline should be started immediately without waiting for confirmatory testing[[/F]], since it is the treatment of choice and a reliable early diagnostic test is often unavailable [1][2][20]. A reported regimen is doxycycline 100 mg twice daily [3].

## Efficacy
- **First-line agent:** Doxycycline is consistently identified as the treatment of choice for scrub typhus across sources [1][2][3][13][18], and is associated with rapid clinical improvement [13]. Azithromycin is also an effective option [7][10].
- **Systematic review evidence:** A Cochrane-level review found tetracycline, doxycycline, azithromycin, and rifampicin are effective with few treatment failures, though [[R]]overall certainty of evidence was graded low[[/R]] [7]. Chloramphenicol remains an option but was excluded from direct comparisons in that review [7].
- **Severe disease — combination therapy:** The [[F]]INTREST randomized trial[[/F]] found IV doxycycline plus azithromycin significantly reduced the primary composite outcome versus either monotherapy: 33% (combination) vs 47% with doxycycline alone (13.3 percentage-point reduction; p=0.002), and vs 48% with azithromycin alone (14.8 percentage-point reduction; p<0.001) [6][11][12]. This trial supports combination therapy specifically in **severe** scrub typhus [4][5][9].
- **Mild vs severe distinction:** One study recommendation (Thailand, 2009) proposed doxycycline alone for mild cases, and doxycycline plus a broad-spectrum agent (cefotaxime/ceftriaxone) for suspected severe cases or diagnostic uncertainty (e.g., co-endemic typhoid/sepsis) [8].
- Early treatment initiation is emphasized to avert life-threatening complications [19][22].

| Regimen | Setting supported | Reported outcome | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Doxycycline monotherapy | Mild/uncomplicated, first-line empiric | Treatment of choice; rapid improvement | [1][2][13][18] |
| Doxycycline 100 mg BD | Case with eschar, clinical suspicion | Empirically started, continued as drug of choice | [3] |
| IV doxycycline + azithromycin | Severe scrub typhus | Primary outcome events 33% vs 47% (doxy alone) vs 48% (azithro alone) | [6][11][12] |
| Doxycycline + ceftriaxone/cefotaxime | Severe disease or diagnostic uncertainty (co-endemic typhoid/sepsis) | Recommended combination (2009 Thailand study) | [8] |

## Safety & adverse effects
- The INTREST trial found combination therapy did **not** increase adverse effects compared with monotherapy [5]; a separate meta-analysis similarly found no difference in clinical failure, mortality, or treatment-related adverse effects between arms compared [24].
- Chloramphenicol was historically used but has been largely discontinued due to toxic side effects [9].
- Doxycycline can be used in persons of any age [21].

## Population
- Findings apply to patients with clinically suspected or confirmed scrub typhus, presenting with fever, headache, myalgia, and/or eschar [17], transmitted via chigger (trombiculid mite) bites [16][25].
- Disease spectrum ranges from mild self-limiting fever to severe multi-organ dysfunction (liver, kidney, lung, CNS) [27]; combination therapy evidence specifically applies to **severe** disease [4][5][6][9].
- Case-level evidence includes a patient with multiorgan involvement (pulmonary edema, pleural effusion) managed with IV doxycycline plus azithromycin plus supportive care (oxygen, ventilatory support), with complete recovery [14][15][26].
- No findings specify subgroup exclusions (e.g., pregnancy) or India-specific national treatment guideline (ICMR/NVBDCP) recommendations.

## Evidence quality
- [[R]]Highest-tier evidence[[/R]]: a Cochrane-level systematic review/meta-analysis on antibiotic efficacy [7], and a named randomized controlled trial (INTREST) on combination therapy in severe disease [5][6][11][12].
- Supporting evidence includes CDC guidance [2][18][20][21][22] and a case report describing empiric doxycycline use guided by eschar and clinical suspicion [3], plus a case of severe disease managed with combination therapy [14][15][26] — these are lower-tier (case-level) but consistent with the higher-tier sources.
- The review notes evidence certainty is "generally low" despite showing efficacy with few treatment failures [7], and the meta-analysis found no arm difference in failure/mortality/adverse effects [24].

## Not addressed
The findings do not include India-specific national treatment guideline (e.g., ICMR/NVBDCP) recommendations, nor address dosing/regimen specifics for pediatric, pregnant, or other special populations, nor confirmatory diagnostic testing protocols for this specific presentation.

## Bottom line
For a newly diagnosed adult with multibacillary (MB) leprosy, start the WHO 3-drug multidrug therapy (MDT) regimen — [[F]]rifampicin, dapsone and clofazimine[[/F]] — and continue it for [[F]]12 months[[/F]] [1][2][10][12][13].

## Regimen (adult MB-MDT)
| Drug | Dose | Frequency |
|---|---|---|
| Rifampicin | 600 mg | Once a month [2] |
| Clofazimine | 300 mg once a month **plus** 50 mg daily [2] | Monthly + daily [2] |
| Dapsone | 100 mg | Daily [2] |

Total duration: **12 months** [1][2][10][12][13]. This is the same 3-drug combination used for all leprosy patients, with duration differentiated by disease type (6 months for paucibacillary vs 12 months for MB) [1][13].

[[K]]MDT must never be given as monotherapy with any single one of these drugs — using only one anti-leprosy drug leads to development of drug resistance[[/K]] [3]. WHO supplies MDT free of cost [15].

## Efficacy
The findings do not report a trial-level cure or relapse rate for standard first-line MB-MDT itself; they establish it as the WHO-recommended regimen [1][10][12] and note a case example where MB-MDT produced "complete lesion resolution" [17]. Separately, in a subgroup at genetic risk of dapsone hypersensitivity (HLA-B*13:01-positive), a retrospective cohort study found a dapsone-free alternative regimen (rifampicin + clofazimine ± clarithromycin/ofloxacin/minocycline) had cure rates "comparable" to standard MDT in HLA-B*13:01-negative patients: [[F]]67.6% vs. 65.8% cure at Year 5, smear negativity 71.43% vs. 75.00% at Year 5, relapse 0.46 vs. 0.20 per 100 person-years[[/F]] [7]. This does not directly quantify efficacy of the standard 3-drug regimen in a general MB population.

## Safety & adverse effects
| Drug | Reported effects |
|---|---|
| Rifampicin (monthly) | No toxic effects reported at monthly dosing; transient reddish urine discoloration for a few hours [4] |
| Clofazimine | Well tolerated, "virtually non-toxic" at MDT doses; reversible brownish-black skin discoloration and dryness that resolves months after stopping [5]; most active when given daily [5][14] |
| Dapsone | Very safe, side effects rare; main risk is allergic reaction (itchy rash, exfoliative dermatitis); avoid in known sulpha-drug allergy [6] |

[[K]]A specific high-risk subgroup — HLA-B*13:01-positive MB patients — is at elevated risk of dapsone hypersensitivity syndrome[[/K]], and for them a dapsone-free alternative (rifampicin + clofazimine ± additional agents) has shown comparable outcomes to standard MDT in HLA-B*13:01-negative patients [7].

During treatment, [[K]]lepra reactions should be watched for and managed, but MDT should NOT be stopped during a reaction[[/K]] [8]. Household contacts should be examined and eligible contacts offered single-dose rifampicin chemoprophylaxis [9].

## Population
These recommendations apply to leprosy (Hansen's disease, caused by *Mycobacterium leprae*) patients classified as multibacillary [16]; duration and drug set differ from paucibacillary disease (6 months) [1][13]. The dapsone-free alternative applies specifically to HLA-B*13:01-positive MB patients at risk of dapsone hypersensitivity, not the general MB population [7]. The findings do not specify age-based dosing adjustments beyond "adult" dosing given [2].

## Evidence quality
- The core MDT recommendation (drugs, doses, 12-month duration) is sourced to **WHO Guidelines for the diagnosis, treatment and prevention of leprosy (2018)** [1][2][13] and is echoed as current WHO guidance [10] and in India-applicable clinical guidance [12] — this is guideline-level evidence, the highest tier.
- Management points on lepra reactions and contact chemoprophylaxis derive from India-specific guideline material [8][9], directly relevant to practice in India; no international/WHO source among the findings contradicts these points.
- [[R]]The HLA-B*13:01 dapsone-free alternative data come from a single retrospective cohort study, not a randomized trial or guideline — this is observational, subgroup-specific evidence and ranks below the WHO/guideline recommendation for standard MB-MDT[[/R]] [7].
- The "complete lesion resolution" statement is a single case-level observation [17], not generalizable efficacy evidence.

## Not addressed
The findings do not give population-level cure, relapse, or completion/adherence rates for standard 3-drug MB-MDT in a general adult population, nor do they address dosing modifications for renal/hepatic impairment, pregnancy, or pediatric patients.

on.question: 5-year-old with high fever from an area with both malaria and dengue. Rapid test shows P. falciparum. Treatment per national policy?

must_have: Artemisinin-based combination therapy (artesunate + sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine in most states; artemether-lumefantrine in the Northeast) for uncomplicated falciparum
Single-dose primaquine as gametocytocidal on day 2 (dose per policy)
Severe malaria requires parenteral artesunate

on.answer:
## Bottom line
For a 5‑year‑old with high fever in a malaria‑ and dengue‑endemic area whose rapid diagnostic test is positive for **P. falciparum**, WHO‑aligned national policy is to treat with an **artemisinin‑based combination therapy (ACT)** — e.g., artemether‑lumefantrine — as first‑line therapy for uncomplicated disease [1][3], initiated promptly given the risk of progression to severe malaria [17][10]. The findings do not include India‑specific (NVBDCP) treatment guidance by name, so this answer rests on WHO global policy and other national programmes' ACT-based guidelines [1][4][5][6].

## Efficacy
- **First-line regimen:** WHO recommends treating uncomplicated *P. falciparum* malaria in children (except first‑trimester pregnant women) with one of five ACTs — artemether‑lumefantrine, artesunate‑amodiaquine, artesunate‑mefloquine, dihydroartemisinin‑piperaquine, or artesunate‑sulfadoxine‑pyrimethamine [1][3]. [[F]]ACT courses must provide 3 days of an artemisinin derivative[[/F]] [2].
- **Dosing for young/small children:** if dihydroartemisinin‑piperaquine is used, children weighing <25 kg should receive at least 2.5 mg/kg/day dihydroartemisinin and 20 mg/kg/day piperaquine for 3 days [15]. Infants <5 kg are treated at the same mg/kg target dose as 5 kg children [9][4].
- **Reported clinical outcomes:** A randomized trial in children reported [[F]]ACT efficacy of 100% with artesunate‑amodiaquine (ASAQ) and 99.1% with artemether‑lumefantrine (AL)[[/F]] for uncomplicated P. falciparum, with equivalent response rates in children <5 years vs older children [8][13].
- Uncomplicated cases can alternatively be treated with atovaquone‑proguanil, with quinine‑based regimens as an alternative option, per some guidance [11].
- Mefloquine-containing regimens are not recommended where infections are acquired in parts of Southeast Asia due to resistance [16] — relevant if travel history is mixed.

## Safety & adverse effects
- In the ACT efficacy trial, **mild and moderate adverse events occurred in 13.3% of patients** [14][8]; no further adverse event detail (severity grading, specific reactions) is given in the findings.
- Weight‑based dosing caps apply: pediatric ACT dosing should never exceed the adult dose, and agents such as artemether‑lumefantrine and atovaquone‑proguanil are only usable in children ≥5 kg per some guidance, with infants <5 kg dosed at the 5 kg mg/kg target [7][9].

## Population
- Applies to **children and adults with uncomplicated P. falciparum malaria** (except first‑trimester pregnant women) [1]. [[K]]Findings on the 5‑year‑old population specifically show that trial response rates were equivalent between children under 5 and older children[[/K]] [8].
- National guidelines reviewed (Ghana, Tanzania, Sudan, Uganda) align with WHO ACT recommendations, with country‑specific first-/second-line choices and weight/age cut-offs for infants <5 kg [4][5][6][9].
- [[K]]Suspected or confirmed P. falciparum malaria — regardless of coexisting dengue exposure — should be managed as a medical emergency[[/K]] [10], and treatment should start with the most readily available recommended regimen without delay because of risk of progression to severe disease [17].
- The findings note severe P. falciparum malaria can present with fever, chills and multi-organ dysfunction, sometimes with early GI features [18], and that bone marrow exam can aid diagnosis in severe/complicated cases with low peripheral parasitemia [20][19] — relevant only if the child's presentation suggests severe disease, not addressed as the scenario given here (uncomplicated, RDT-positive).

## Evidence quality
- The core treatment recommendation comes from **WHO guidance**, the top of the evidence hierarchy for this question, corroborated by a review noting WHO recommends six ACTs as first-line for P. falciparum [1][3][12].
- Country-level guideline comparisons (Ghana, Tanzania, Uganda, Sudan) are drawn from a review of national policies, showing consistent alignment with WHO [4][5][6].
- [[R]]The 100%/99.1% efficacy and 13.3% adverse-event figures come from a single randomized trial in children — a controlled, higher-tier study for efficacy, but one trial, not a systematic review, and its resistance/geographic context is not specified in these findings[[/R]] [8][13][14].
- No findings on dengue co-endemicity or India-specific national treatment guidelines were retrieved; the analysis relies on WHO/other national programme policy for practice extrapolation.

## Not addressed
The findings do not include **India-specific (e.g., NVBDCP/ICMR) national treatment guidelines** by name, nor any guidance on managing a patient in an area of overlapping malaria–dengue risk (e.g., differentiating co-infection, or altering malaria treatment because of dengue exposure). These are evidence gaps, not clinical conclusions.

on.question: HIV-positive adult, newly diagnosed, asymptomatic. When do we start TB preventive treatment in India and with what?

must_have: TPT is indicated for people living with HIV after active TB is ruled out
6 months of isoniazid (6H) or shorter rifapentine-based regimens (e.g. 3HP) per current national guidance
Pyridoxine co-administration with isoniazid

on.answer:
## Bottom line
In India's NTEP/PMTPT programme, an HIV-positive adult who is newly diagnosed and asymptomatic should be screened to rule out active TB, and — once active TB is excluded — started on TB preventive treatment (TPT) as part of the HIV care package [1][2][8], using a programme regimen such as **6 months of daily isoniazid (6H)** or a shorter **rifamycin-based regimen (e.g., 3HP weekly isoniazid–rifapentine)** [2][3], with **1HP and 3RH** also available as additional NTEP-endorsed options [4].

## Efficacy / When to start
- [[K]]People living with HIV (adults, adolescents, children >12 months, and HIV-exposed infants <12 months in contact with active TB) are a prioritized target group for TPT under NTEP[[/K]] [1].
- TPT is to be offered **after ruling out active TB disease** — this exclusion step is a prerequisite, not optional, for both household contacts and PLHIV [2][8].
- The Indian PMTPT cascade-of-care model requires **screening all PLHIV** and providing TPT only once active TB has been excluded, as part of the continuum of HIV/TB care [8].
- WHO consolidated guidance (informing national policy) states adults/adolescents living with HIV who are **unlikely to have active TB** should receive TPT as part of a comprehensive HIV care package, [[F]]irrespective of degree of immunosuppression and even when TB-infection testing is unavailable[[/F]] [5][13]; this applies also to those already on ART, pregnant women, and those previously treated for TB [5][14].
- Regimen options under the Indian programme:
  | Regimen | Description | Source |
  |---|---|---|
  | 6H | 6 months daily isoniazid | [2][3] |
  | 3HP | Weekly isoniazid–rifapentine, shorter rifamycin-based course | [2][3] |
  | 1HP | Addendum regimen to national PMTPT guidelines | [4] |
  | 3RH | Addendum regimen to national PMTPT guidelines | [4] |
- Older isoniazid-preventive-therapy labeling (reflecting the classic IPT rationale) recommends isoniazid for HIV-infected persons, including those who are tuberculin-negative but from high-TB-prevalence groups [6][9], with a **minimum of 12 months of therapy** for HIV-infected candidates [10] — this figure comes from historical US product labeling, not the current Indian 6H/3HP programme regimens [2][3].
- Isoniazid monotherapy has shown efficacy in preventing TB across multiple populations historically, which underlies the 6-month IPT regimen's adoption [11].

## Safety & adverse effects
- **Isoniazid (6H):** asymptomatic elevation of liver enzymes, hepatitis, peripheral neuropathy (paresthesia, numbness, limb pain), skin rash, sleepiness/lethargy [7].
- **Rifapentine (3HP):** gastrointestinal reactions (abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting), hypersensitivity reactions (flu-like symptoms), hepatitis, discoloration of body fluids [7].
- No comparative adverse-event rates or head-to-head safety data between 6H, 3HP, 1HP, and 3RH are given in the findings.

## Population
- Applies to adults, adolescents, and children >12 months living with HIV on ART, and HIV-exposed infants <12 months in contact with active TB, under NTEP [1].
- WHO guidance extends the "start TPT" recommendation to PLHIV on ART, pregnant women, and those previously treated for TB, regardless of immunosuppression level, even without TB-infection testing [5][14] — consistent with the asymptomatic, newly diagnosed adult in the question.
- All recommendations presuppose active TB has first been excluded [2][8]; the findings do not address what to do differently if the patient has symptoms suggestive of active TB.

## Evidence quality
- [[R]]Indian national programme guidance (NTEP/PMTPT) [1][2][3][4][8] is programme-level policy for India and is the directly applicable source for practice in India; WHO consolidated guidelines [5][13][14] are the international guideline tier informing this policy.[[/R]]
- The 12-month isoniazid-duration and tuberculin-negative recommendations [6][9][10] derive from older US product labeling rather than a systematic review or the current Indian programme guidance, and predate/differ from the 6H/3HP regimens specified in Indian guidance [2][3] — this is a lower-tier, historical source relative to current national/WHO guidance.
- The isoniazid-efficacy statement [11] and implementation-barrier statement [12] derive from a narrative/summary source (europepmc), not a specific randomized trial with reported effect sizes.
- No completed phase 3 trial results, systematic review effect sizes, or comparative regimen efficacy data (e.g., TB incidence rates by regimen) are present in the findings.

## Not addressed
The findings do not provide a specific TB-infection testing algorithm (e.g., TST/IGRA use before TPT) for India, quantitative TB-incidence-reduction figures for 6H vs 3HP vs 1HP vs 3RH, or guidance on management if the patient is found to have active TB rather than being TPT-eligible.
